traveler: Alexandre Gustave Bonickhausen dit Eiffel (Gustave Eiffel)
title: The Arch Stood Upright: Bordeaux, the Douro, Garabit, and Three Hundred Metres over the Champ de Mars
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Dijon, the birth on the Cote-d'Or
stops.date_confidence: attested (fr.wikipedia, en.wikipedia)
stops.campa: In Dijon a son is born to Alexandre Bonickhausen dit Eiffel, an officer of military supply, and Catherine-Melanie Moneuse, who runs a coal business of her own and runs it better than her husband ran his commission. They name him Alexandre Gustave. The second surname is a French mouth's version of the Eifel hills in the Rhineland, from which an ancestor came generations back; the first is German enough to cost a man contracts. Fifty years on he will go to court to have it struck off. The coal money pays for the schooling.
suggested_refs: The Eiffel birth house in Dijon; the exact street address is not confirmed in the sources reached

stops.name: Paris, the College Sainte-Barbe
stops.date_confidence: year attested (fr.wikipedia); month and day unknown, defaulted to 01-01
stops.campa: Sent up from Dijon with his baccalaureat in hand, he boards at the College Sainte-Barbe on the rue Valette, the cramming house that feeds the grandes ecoles. The target is the Ecole Polytechnique, which makes state engineers and marshals of France. He does not get in. He is admitted instead to the Ecole Centrale des Arts et Manufactures, which trains men for industry rather than for the state. The tower will be built by a private contractor with his own workshops, not by a servant of the Republic.
suggested_refs: The College Sainte-Barbe, 4 rue Valette, Paris

stops.name: Paris, the Hotel Sale and the Ecole Centrale
stops.date_confidence: graduation year attested (en.wikipedia); month unknown, defaulted. Location corrected: the school occupied the Hotel Sale, 5 rue de Thorigny, from 1829 to 1884, not the later Ecole Centrale site the research pool gave
stops.campa: The Ecole Centrale occupies the Hotel Sale in the Marais, a seventeenth-century salt-tax mansion given over to furnaces and drawing boards. Eiffel graduates thirteenth of eighty. His speciality is chemistry, not iron; an uncle's vinegar works in Dijon is the career his family expects, and a family quarrel closes it. He goes looking for work in Paris with a chemist's diploma and no bridge to his name. Every wrought-iron arch he will later throw across a gorge is drawn by a man trained to think about materials rather than about structures.
suggested_refs: The Hotel Sale, 5 rue de Thorigny, seat of the Ecole Centrale des Arts et Manufactures 1829-1884

segments.name: The Garonne and the First Iron

stops.name: Paris, Charles Nepveu and the trade of metal
stops.date_confidence: year attested (fr.wikipedia); month unknown, defaulted
stops.campa: Through a family connection he meets Charles Nepveu, a builder of railway equipment in metal, and takes work in his office. Nepveu goes bankrupt within a year; the business passes to a Belgian firm, the Compagnie Belge de Materiels de Chemin de Fer, and Nepveu keeps the young man on as head of the research department. Eiffel learns the trade in the collapse of the man who taught it to him. He is twenty-four and has now seen, from the inside, how an iron company dies of its own contracts.
suggested_refs: Charles Nepveu's Paris office and the records of the Compagnie Belge de Materiels de Chemin de Fer

stops.name: Bordeaux, the bridge over the Garonne
stops.date_confidence: contested. fr.wikipedia dates his involvement from 1858 and calls it his first major project at twenty-six; en.wikipedia dates the works 1857-1860 and has him take over site management from Nepveu only in March 1860, aged twenty-seven. Not resolved. Coordinates corrected: the Passerelle Eiffel is at 44.8322/-0.5522, not the 44.8478 the research pool gave, which lands near the Pont Chaban-Delmas
stops.campa: The Compagnie Belge takes the contract for a railway bridge across the Garonne at Bordeaux, some five hundred metres of iron on six piers, and sends Eiffel to the river. The piers are sunk by compressed-air caisson, a method barely tested in France, and set true with hydraulic rams. A workman falls in the current and Eiffel goes in after him. Nepveu hands him the site in March of 1860, and the bridge that opens that year carries his reputation as surely as it carries the trains. The Republic lists it as a historic monument in 2010.
suggested_refs: The Passerelle Eiffel at Bordeaux, listed monument historique 2010 after campaigning by the Association of the Descendants of Gustave Eiffel

stops.name: Dijon, the marriage to Marguerite Gaudelet
stops.date_confidence: attested (fr.wikipedia)
stops.campa: He comes back to Dijon to marry Marguerite Gaudelet, seventeen years old, of a family known to his own. Five children follow. Claire is born the next year, Edouard in 1866. Marguerite keeps the household in Paris while her husband is on rivers in three countries and on the Egyptian coast. Claire will take the house over at fourteen, when her mother is gone, and she will still be running it when her father dies an old man sixty-one years from this altar.
suggested_refs: The Eiffel-Gaudelet marriage register, Dijon, 7 April 1862

stops.name: Suez, the canal of Ferdinand de Lesseps
stops.date_confidence: year attested (en.wikipedia); month unknown, defaulted
stops.campa: A locomotive contract for the Egyptian government takes him to Egypt, and while he is there he goes to look at the ditch the French are cutting between two seas. Ferdinand de Lesseps has been digging it for seven years and will open it in three more, the largest engineering fame in France. Eiffel is thirty-three and unknown outside the trade. Twenty-one years later de Lesseps will hire him to build the locks of a second canal, at Panama, and the two names will go into the same courtroom together.
suggested_refs: The Suez Canal works under construction, 1866, visited during the Egyptian locomotive contract

stops.name: Levallois-Perret, the workshops on the rue Fouquet
stops.date_confidence: year attested (fr.wikipedia); month unknown, defaulted
stops.campa: He borrows capital, buys the Pauwels workshops at Levallois-Perret on the north-western edge of Paris, and sets up on his own account. Out of these sheds will come, in numbered crates, bridges for Portugal and Hungary and Cochinchina, churches for Peru, lighthouses for the Egyptian coast, gasworks for Bolivia, the skeleton of a statue for New York, and eighteen thousand parts of a tower. He will be buried in the cemetery a few streets away, within sight of the ground where the iron was cut.
suggested_refs: The former Ateliers Pauwels at Levallois-Perret, acquired 1866, the fabrication works behind every later commission

segments.name: Eiffel et Cie: the World Trade in Iron

stops.name: Champ de Mars, the Galerie des Machines
stops.date_confidence: year attested (Wikipedia, 'Gustave Eiffel'); month unknown, defaulted
stops.campa: For the Exposition Universelle of 1867 Jean-Baptiste Krantz takes him on to calculate the arched girders of the Galerie des Machines, the great oval hall on the Champ de Mars. It is his first work on this ground and his first at exhibition scale. The Champ de Mars is a parade field for the military school; it will hold five world's fairs in his lifetime. Twenty-two years from now the tower will stand at its river end, and Luc-Olivier Merson will take a gold medal for painting in its shadow.
suggested_refs: The Galerie des Machines of 1867, Champ de Mars, girders calculated by Eiffel under Jean-Baptiste Krantz

stops.name: Paris, Eiffel et Cie founded with Seyrig
stops.date_confidence: attested (en.wikipedia)
stops.campa: Eiffel signs a partnership with Theophile Seyrig, a Centrale man like himself and the better mathematician of the two, and the firm takes the name Eiffel et Cie. Seyrig does the calculation of arches; Eiffel does the contracts, the sites and the price of iron. The arrangement lasts eleven years and produces the Douro bridge. It ends in a quarrel over who designed that bridge, which is the quarrel the name Eiffel will keep provoking for the rest of his life and long after it.
suggested_refs: The deed of partnership of 6 October 1868 constituting Eiffel et Cie

stops.name: Verdun, the station put into service
stops.date_confidence: the station was built in 1868 to Eiffel's plans, put into service 14 April 1870 and officially inaugurated 1 July 1870; the research pool's wording, 'completed', is wrong for this date. Coordinates corrected from 49.1593/5.3822 (about 0.7 km off) to 49.1656/5.3794
stops.campa: The railway station at Verdun, built two years earlier to Eiffel's plans, takes its first trains in April and is inaugurated formally at midsummer. Four months after that the Second Empire is gone and the Prussians are on the Meuse. The station is a modest thing beside the arches he is already drawing for Portugal, and it stands where the twentieth century will grind the French army for ten months. He is building the ordinary furniture of the railway age, and the ground is not ordinary.
suggested_refs: The Gare de Verdun, built 1868 to Eiffel's plans, in service 14 April 1870

stops.name: La Paz, the gasworks in the Andes
stops.date_confidence: year attested (Wikipedia, 'Gustave Eiffel'); month unknown, defaulted
stops.campa: The firm builds gasworks at La Paz, eleven thousand feet up in the Andes, iron shipped from Levallois-Perret to the Pacific and hauled inland. The Peru-Bolivia-Chile coast becomes an Eiffel market: gasworks, the metal frame of the cathedral at Tacna, a cast-iron fountain of the Three Graces for the plaza at Moquegua. Guano and nitrate money pays for French iron, and French iron answers a coast that earthquakes flatten every generation. A building that arrives in crates can be put up again after the next one.
suggested_refs: The La Paz gasworks; the Cathedral of San Pedro at Tacna; the Three Graces fountain at Moquegua

stops.name: Arica, the iron church redirected by an earthquake
stops.date_confidence: the pieces arrive 1875 and the building is inaugurated 1876 (es.wikipedia); month unknown, defaulted. The research pool tagged the attribution [R], but es.wikipedia states plainly that the church was commissioned from Eiffel's workshops, so the doubt is weaker than the tag implies. Coordinates corrected from -18.4783/-70.3126, about 0.9 km off
stops.campa: A prefabricated iron church leaves the Levallois workshops for Ancon, the bathing resort near Lima that President Jose Balta wants furnished. An earthquake in 1868 has meanwhile destroyed the church at Arica, further down the same coast, and the crates are redirected there. The pieces arrive in 1875 and the building is inaugurated the year after. It is bolted iron on a shore of adobe ruins, and it will outlast the tidal waves and the war that takes Arica from Peru and gives it to Chile.
suggested_refs: The Catedral de San Marcos de Arica, prefabricated for Ancon and redirected after the 1868 earthquake
sources: es.wikipedia, 'Catedral de San Marcos de Arica'

stops.name: Levallois-Perret, the death of Marguerite
stops.date_confidence: the research pool tags this [R]; fr.wikipedia gives 8 September 1877 at Levallois-Perret, aged 32
stops.campa: Marguerite Eiffel dies at Levallois-Perret at thirty-two, fifteen years married, her children still small. Eiffel is forty-four and does not marry again. Claire, fourteen years old, takes over the running of the house and keeps it for forty-six years, until he dies in it. She is buried in the autumn; in Portugal the Douro arch is closing and in Budapest the train shed is finishing. The man does not stop. What the loss costs him is a gap in the record, not a thing the sources describe.
suggested_refs: The Eiffel family vault at Levallois-Perret, opened for Marguerite in 1877

stops.name: Budapest, the Nyugati train shed
stops.date_confidence: opening date attested (en.wikipedia); the contract dates to 1875
stops.campa: The Western station opens at Budapest, its train shed a glazed iron hall with the tracks running under glass to a wall of window at the street end. Eiffel et Cie builds it. The design is credited to the architect Auguste de Serres, and the popular attribution of the whole station to Eiffel is one of the earliest cases of a habit that will fasten his name to iron buildings on four continents, some of them his and some of them not. The firm is now taking work from governments rather than from contractors.
suggested_refs: Nyugati palyaudvar, Budapest, opened 28 October 1877, designed by Auguste de Serres and built by Eiffel et Cie

stops.name: Porto, the arch over the Douro
stops.date_confidence: opening attested (en.wikipedia). The competition was won in 1875, but on-site construction ran 5 January 1876 to 1 October 1877; the research pool's '1875-05' conflated the award with a construction start. Coordinates corrected from 41.1372/-8.6076, about 0.9 km off
stops.campa: King Luis I and Queen Maria Pia open the railway bridge that carries her name across the gorge of the Douro. Eiffel et Cie won the competition in 1875 with the lowest bid, 965,000 francs, and built a single wrought-iron arch of some one hundred and sixty metres over water too deep and too fast for piers. The arch is raised from both banks at once and closed in the middle over nothing at all. It is the form he will build again, larger, over the Truyere, and again, doubled and turned upright, at the feet of the tower.
suggested_refs: The Ponte Maria Pia over the Douro, built 5 January 1876 to 1 October 1877, opened 4 November 1877

stops.name: Champ de Mars, the Gas Company pavilion
stops.date_confidence: year attested (Wikipedia, 'Gustave Eiffel'); month unknown, defaulted
stops.campa: For the Exposition of 1878, held on this same field, he designs a pavilion for the Paris Gas Company and takes on an architect to dress it, Stephen Sauvestre. Sauvestre is the man who will later put arches, a glass hall and an ornamented first platform onto Koechlin's bare pylon and make it a thing Paris can be asked to accept. The engineer has learned that a structure calculated correctly still has to be looked at by people who cannot read a calculation.
suggested_refs: The Paris Gas Company pavilion, Exposition Universelle 1878, first Eiffel-Sauvestre collaboration

stops.name: Paris, Seyrig goes and Koechlin comes
stops.date_confidence: year attested for both the dissolution and Koechlin's arrival (en.wikipedia, fr.wikipedia); months unknown, defaulted
stops.campa: The partnership with Seyrig dissolves after the quarrel over the Douro, and the house is renamed the Compagnie des Etablissements Eiffel. In the same year a young Swiss engineer out of Zurich, Maurice Koechlin, joins the design office and takes over the calculation of arches. Emile Nouguier is already there. Those two will draw, five years from now, a pylon of four lattice legs curving in to a point, and Eiffel's name will go on the patent beside their own and then stay on it alone.
suggested_refs: The design office of the Compagnie des Etablissements Eiffel, Levallois-Perret, under Koechlin and Nouguier

stops.name: Paris, the judgment on the name
stops.date_confidence: a decree of 1879 and a civil judgment of 15 December 1880 are both cited by fr.wikipedia; the relation between the two acts is not spelled out in the sources reached
stops.campa: A decree of 1879 and a civil judgment of December 1880 authorise the family to drop Bonickhausen and be Eiffel alone. The argument put to the court is commercial: a German-sounding name raises doubt about a Frenchman's nationality nine years after Sedan, and doubt of that kind costs money. He is forty-eight, and the name the court has just made lawful is already bolted into bridges in six countries. It is the trademark, not the man, that is being registered as French.
stops.quote: une consonance allemande qui inspire [des] doutes sur [sa] nationalité française, et ce simple doute est de nature à [lui] causer, soit individuellement, soit commercialement, le plus grand préjudice
stops.quote_source: Gustave Eiffel, cited in fr.wikipedia 'Gustave Eiffel', n. 3. The editorial brackets are in the source and are retained here: the underlying original is presumably first person, and the primary document (petition or letter) was not located.
suggested_refs: The 1879 decree and the civil judgment of 15 December 1880 on the surname Bonickhausen dit Eiffel

stops.name: Rue de Chazelles, the pylon under the copper
stops.date_confidence: Bartholdi's approach is dated 1881 by en.wikipedia 'Gustave Eiffel' and 1880 by en.wikipedia 'Statue of Liberty'; not resolved. The Paris assembly is complete by July 1884 and dismantling begins January 1885. Month of the 1884 assembly stage defaulted
stops.campa: Auguste Bartholdi has a copper woman forty-six metres tall and no way to hold her up in the wind off New York harbour. Viollet-le-Duc, the architect serving as the project's chief engineer, meant to ballast her with sand. He is dead. Eiffel gives her a four-legged iron pylon with a flexible secondary frame, so the skin can move against the frame in frost and in gale without tearing. The whole statue is assembled in the yard at the rue de Chazelles, higher than the roofs, and the quarter watches her go up and then come down again for shipping.
suggested_refs: The Eiffel works at 25 rue de Chazelles, where the Statue of Liberty was assembled entire before shipment

stops.name: Ruynes-en-Margeride, the arch over the Truyere
stops.date_confidence: contract 1879, arch closed 1884, opened to traffic November 1885; month of closure unknown, defaulted. Coordinates corrected to 44.97528/3.17750: the research pool gave three different and all incorrect pairs for Garabit across its three lenses. Height given as 124 m by en.wikipedia and 122.5 m elsewhere
stops.campa: The Garabit viaduct closes its arch over the gorge of the Truyere in the Cantal: one hundred and sixty-five metres of span, the rail deck some one hundred and twenty-four metres above the water, the tallest bridge in the world. Leon Boyer laid out the crossing; Eiffel's office, with Nouguier and Koechlin, builds the arch on the Douro principle enlarged. Nothing supports it from beneath while it goes up. The line opens to traffic in November 1885, and the drawing office that has just done this is about to be asked what it can do standing up.
suggested_refs: The Garabit Viaduct, classified monument historique 2017, candidate for UNESCO World Heritage listing since 2018

stops.name: Liberty Island, the armature dedicated
stops.date_confidence: dedication date attested (fr.wikipedia); the research pool's chronology lens gives the year only
stops.campa: Liberty Enlightening the World is dedicated on Bedloe's Island in New York harbour, Bartholdi's copper on Eiffel's iron. The pylon inside carries every pound of her and lets the skin ride loose upon it. Whether Eiffel crosses the Atlantic for the ceremony is not recorded in the sources reached. French Wikipedia gives the design of the skeleton to Koechlin working under him, English Wikipedia to Eiffel himself, and the two accounts are left here unreconciled. The statue marks a revolution whose centenary his tower will mark in three years.
suggested_refs: The internal armature of the Statue of Liberty, Liberty Island, New York Harbor

stops.name: Paris, the patent of eighteen September
stops.date_confidence: attested (toureiffel.paris official history)
stops.campa: Koechlin and Nouguier bring their chief a drawing made in June: a tall pylon of four lattice uprights, curved, meeting at a point, three hundred metres. Eiffel is cool on it at first and then buys it. On the eighteenth of September the three of them deposit a patent for an arrangement permitting the construction of metal supports and pylons capable of exceeding a height of three hundred metres, and Eiffel purchases his engineers' rights in it outright. The tower will be called by the name on the cheque.
suggested_refs: The patent of 18 September 1884, deposited jointly by Eiffel, Koechlin and Nouguier

stops.name: Paris, the paper to the civil engineers
stops.date_confidence: attested (en.wikipedia, quoting the paper)
stops.campa: Before the Societe des Ingenieurs Civils he argues the tower as a proposition rather than as a structure. Nobody has yet built to three hundred metres. He tells the engineers what the height is for: the Revolution turns a hundred years old in 1889, France means to hold a fair for it, and a tower is the only object that can be seen from every quarter of the city at once. The case he makes is not that iron can reach that high. It is that the century which learned to make iron owes itself a monument.
stops.quote: not only the art of the modern engineer, but also the century of Industry and Science in which we are living, and for which the way was prepared by the great scientific movement of the eighteenth century and by the Revolution of 1789, to which this monument will be built as an expression of France's gratitude
stops.quote_source: Gustave Eiffel, paper to the Societe des Ingenieurs Civils, 30 March 1885, English translation as quoted on en.wikipedia, 'Gustave Eiffel'
suggested_refs: The 30 March 1885 paper to the Societe des Ingenieurs Civils, first public case for the tower

stops.name: Champ de Mars, the foundations opened
stops.date_confidence: 28 January 1887 per en.wikipedia and fr.wikipedia. The research pool's chronology lens gave 26 January and its geography lens 28 January, an internal contradiction; the official figure of two years, two months and five days is what tempts sources toward the 26th
stops.campa: A convention signed on the eighth of January with the State and the City of Paris gives Eiffel a subsidy of one and a half million francs, under a quarter of the cost, and the operating concession for twenty years, after which the tower is to come down. He finds the rest himself. On the twenty-eighth the digging starts at the Champ de Mars: two legs on concrete, two legs on caissons sunk with compressed air below the water table of the Seine, the method he first used on the Garonne thirty years back.
suggested_refs: The convention of 8 January 1887 between Eiffel, the State and the City of Paris

stops.name: Paris, the protest of the three hundred
stops.date_confidence: attested; protest and reply printed in Le Temps the same day
stops.campa: Le Temps prints a letter signed by Maupassant, Dumas fils, Gounod and some three hundred others, protesting in the name of French taste against the useless and monstrous tower. Eiffel's reply runs in the same paper on the same day. He does not argue that the tower is not large. He argues that largeness is a category of beauty for which the signatories have no theory, and asks whether the true conditions of strength are not always the secret conditions of harmony.
stops.quote: To bring our arguments home, imagine for a moment a giddy, ridiculous tower dominating Paris like a gigantic black smokestack, crushing under its barbaric bulk Notre Dame, the Tour Saint-Jacques, the Louvre, the Dome of les Invalides, the Arc de Triomphe, all of our humiliated monuments will disappear in this ghastly dream.
stops.quote_source: Les artistes contre la tour Eiffel, the Committee of Three Hundred petition, Le Temps, 14 February 1887, English translation as quoted on en.wikipedia, 'Eiffel Tower'. Not by Eiffel; this is the text he answered the same day.
suggested_refs: Le Temps, 14 February 1887, carrying both the artists' protest and Eiffel's reply
sources: Gustave Eiffel, Reponse a la protestation des artistes, French Wikisource

stops.name: Place de l'Etoile, the answer from the Arc de Triomphe
stops.date_confidence: attested; the passage is in the reply of 14 February 1887
stops.campa: The protest says the tower will crush Notre-Dame, the Louvre, the Invalides, the Arc de Triomphe, that the monuments of Paris will vanish under its barbarous bulk. Eiffel sends the signatories to the Etoile to look. The Arc de Triomphe is fifty metres high and the houses around the circus are not made smaller by standing next to it. Scale is not a subtraction. This letter is the only sustained piece of aesthetic argument he ever publishes, and he writes it in a fortnight with the foundations open.
stops.quote: Allez au rond-point de l'Étoile, et parce que l'Arc de Triomphe est grand les maisons de la place ne vous en paraîtront pas plus petites.
stops.quote_source: Gustave Eiffel, Reponse de Gustave Eiffel a la protestation des artistes, Le Temps, 14 February 1887 (French Wikisource text)
suggested_refs: The Place de l'Etoile and the Arc de Triomphe, the comparison Eiffel invites his critics to make on foot
sources: Gustave Eiffel, Reponse a la protestation des artistes, Le Temps, 14 February 1887, French Wikisource

stops.name: Champ de Mars, the tricolour at the summit
stops.date_confidence: attested (toureiffel.paris official history)
stops.campa: Two years, two months and five days after the digging began, Eiffel climbs the stairs to the top with a party of officials, the lifts not yet running, and at twenty-five minutes to three raises a tricolour to a salute of twenty-five guns. He is decorated with the Legion of Honour on the platform. Not one workman has died on the structure. Three hundred metres of wrought iron stand over a city that petitioned, in three hundred signatures, against them, and the iron is curved exactly where the wind requires it.
stops.quote: All the cutting force of the wind passes into the interior of the leading edge uprights.
stops.quote_source: Gustave Eiffel on the tower's wind-resistant curvature, English translation as presented on toureiffel.paris, drawn from his writings and later expanded in La Tour de trois cents metres (1900)
suggested_refs: La Tour de trois cents metres (1900), Eiffel's own technical account of the structure

stops.name: Champ de Mars, the fair opens
stops.date_confidence: attested (fr.wikipedia)
stops.campa: The Exposition Universelle opens on the centenary of the Revolution and the tower is its gate. Two million people go up in six months, hauled by hydraulic lifts. Luc-Olivier Merson takes the gold medal for painting in the fine-arts palace beneath it, one of the trade that signed against the iron. Eleven years later Isadora Duncan and Rudolf Laban will walk the next fair on this same field, and the tower will be by then not an argument but simply where they are standing.
stops.quote: Moreover, there is, in the colossal, a unique attraction and charm to which ordinary artistic theories are hardly applicable.
stops.quote_source: Gustave Eiffel, reply to the 1887 artists' protest, English translation as presented on toureiffel.paris official history page
suggested_refs: The Exposition Universelle of 1889, Champ de Mars, with the tower as its monumental entrance arch

stops.name: Panama, the locks of the Compagnie Universelle
stops.date_confidence: year attested (en.wikipedia); month unknown, defaulted. Whether Eiffel travelled to the isthmus, as against directing the lock design from Paris, is not confirmed in the sources reached and is recorded as a gap
stops.campa: De Lesseps, beaten by the isthmus, abandons the sea-level cut and orders locks. Eiffel's company contracts to design and build them, each lifting a ship about eleven metres. The work is done at Levallois-Perret and shipped. Whether Eiffel himself ever stands on the isthmus is not established. He is at this moment raising the tower with one hand and taking the largest contract of his life with the other, from the man whose ditch at Suez he had walked out to admire as an unknown engineer of thirty-three.
suggested_refs: The lock contracts of the Compagnie Universelle du Canal Interoceanique with the Compagnie des Etablissements Eiffel

stops.name: Colon, the payments suspended
stops.date_confidence: attested (en.wikipedia). The suspension is a corporate act taken in Paris; the pin is placed at the Caribbean end of the works, where its effect is visible
stops.campa: The Compagnie Universelle du Canal Interoceanique stops paying interest to its bondholders. Eight hundred thousand French savers had put money into the isthmus. The works halt, the machines rust in the cut, and the scandal that follows brings down ministers and makes careers for anti-Semites in the Paris press. Mikhail Bakunin crossed this coast by rail in 1861 and Eadweard Muybridge photographed the same railway in 1875, when the canal was still an idea. Aime Tschiffely will ride past the finished American one in 1928.
suggested_refs: The Panama scandal papers, 1888-1893; the abandoned French works at Colon and the Culebra cut

stops.name: Iquitos, the iron house up the Amazon
stops.date_confidence: attribution disputed and left disputed. es.wikipedia credits the design to Eiffel around 1860 and the fabrication to the Belgian Forges d'Aiseau; the house was shown at the 1889 Paris Exposition and reached Iquitos in 1890 aboard the Brazilian ship Perseveranca. The research pool's '1889-1892' and its 'another Parisian iron-house manufacturer' are both wrong. Month unknown, defaulted
stops.campa: An entirely prefabricated iron house, shown at the Paris Exposition of 1889 under the new tower, is bought by a rubber baron, shipped in pieces to the Amazon aboard the Brazilian steamer Perseveranca, and bolted together at Iquitos. The town calls it the Casa de Fierro and calls it Eiffel's. Spanish Wikipedia gives the design to Eiffel around 1860 and the fabrication to the Belgian works Forges d'Aiseau. The attribution is disputed. It is recorded here as disputed, which is what the name Eiffel has now become: a category of object.
suggested_refs: The Casa de Fierro on the Plaza de Armas at Iquitos, Peru

stops.name: Munchenstein, the bridge over the Birs
stops.date_confidence: attested (en.wikipedia). Corrections to the research pool: seventy-three killed, not seventy-one, and the bridge was built by Eiffel et Cie itself in 1874-75, not by 'Eiffel's former associates'. Coordinates corrected to 47.5177/7.6183
stops.campa: A train on the Jura-Simplon line crosses the Birs at Munchenstein near Basel and the bridge goes down under it. Seventy-three people are killed and one hundred and seventy-one seriously hurt, the worst railway disaster Switzerland has known. The bridge was built by Eiffel et Cie in 1874 and 1875. The inquiry advances the science of buckling in iron lattice, and it also lays the name of the tower's builder on a heap of dead, eighteen months before the Panama trial opens.
suggested_refs: The Munchenstein rail disaster inquiry of 1891 and its findings on lattice-girder buckling

stops.name: Paris, the Palais de Justice
stops.date_confidence: attested (en.wikipedia, fr.wikipedia)
stops.campa: Tried over the money of the canal company, Eiffel is convicted of misuse of funds, fined twenty thousand francs and sentenced to two years in prison. He never serves a day. The Court of Cassation quashes the conviction on the ground that the offence was time-barred, not on the ground that it did not occur, and his defenders and his accusers have both been careful about that distinction ever since. Pierre Waldeck-Rousseau is among his counsel. The Legion of Honour council threatens to resign in a body rather than strip his cross.
suggested_refs: The Panama trial record, Palais de Justice, Paris, February 1893, and the subsequent Cassation ruling

stops.name: Paris, the general meeting
stops.date_confidence: attested (en.wikipedia). The research pool's geography lens says he resigned before the verdict; he announced the intention before the trial, but the resignation was formalised at the general meeting five days after it
stops.campa: Five days after the verdict, at the general meeting of his company, Eiffel resigns from the board. The house he founded in 1866 goes on without him in its direction and under a changed name. He is sixty, rich, and finished as a builder of public works. During these years several French towns take his name off their streets, and later put it back. He does not build another bridge. What he does with the next thirty years is decided in this week, and it is decided upward.
stops.quote: I have absolutely decided to abstain from any participation in any manufacturing business from now on.
stops.quote_source: Gustave Eiffel, statement at the General Meeting regarding the Panama Canal affair, 14 February 1893, English translation as quoted on en.wikipedia, 'Gustave Eiffel'
suggested_refs: Minutes of the general meeting of 14 February 1893 at which Eiffel left the board

stops.name: Champ de Mars, the observatory at the summit
stops.date_confidence: the 1898 meteorological installation is tagged [R] in the research pool and rests on fr.wikipedia alone; month unknown, defaulted. Eugene Ducretet's wireless experiment from the summit to the Pantheon on 5 November 1898 is separately attested
stops.campa: The concession runs out in 1909, and the tower is then to be taken down and sold for scrap. Eiffel sets about making it indispensable. He installs meteorological instruments at the top and publishes the readings; the summit becomes the highest observation post in Europe, measuring wind, pressure and the fall of temperature with height. In November Eugene Ducretet sends a wireless signal from the top to the Pantheon. The tower stops being a monument and starts being an instrument, which is a thing a city does not scrap.
suggested_refs: The meteorological station on the third level of the Eiffel Tower and its published observations

stops.name: Borjomi, the bridge over the Tsemistskali
stops.date_confidence: year attested (Wikipedia, 'Gustave Eiffel'); month unknown, defaulted
stops.campa: A bridge to Eiffel's design goes up over the Tsemistskali at Borjomi in the Caucasus, in the mineral-water valley the Romanovs use as a summer resort. It is among the furthest-flung works carried out to the firm's drawings after he leaves it. His name now travels on a catalogue rather than on a site visit: the plans sit on file at Levallois-Perret, a governor in Tiflis can order from them, and the engineer whose name is bolted into the girders is in Paris measuring wind.
suggested_refs: The Eiffel bridge over the Tsemistskali at Borjomi, Georgia

stops.name: Champ de Mars, the wireless station
stops.date_confidence: the permanent military wireless station is Gustave Ferrie's, 1903, per fr.wikipedia; the research pool's '1901 permanent transmitter' does not exist. Month unknown, defaulted
stops.campa: Captain Gustave Ferrie persuades the army to put a permanent military wireless station on the tower, and Eiffel pays for the aerials himself. From 1903 the summit talks to the eastern forts, then further. When the concession lapses in 1909 the City of Paris does not take the tower down, because the army will not give up the mast. The structure survives on the ground of utility, exactly as its builder argued in 1887 that structures should be judged. A radio aerial answers the artists of 1887, and the letter to Le Temps does not.
suggested_refs: Gustave Ferrie's military wireless station on the Eiffel Tower, established 1903

stops.name: Champ de Mars, the first wind tunnel
stops.date_confidence: year attested (en.wikipedia, fr.wikipedia); month unknown, defaulted
stops.campa: At the foot of the tower he builds a laboratory, and inside it a wind tunnel: a tube through which a fan drives air past a suspended model. He had begun by dropping shapes on a guided cable from the second platform and weighing their resistance as they fell. Now he brings the air to the object instead of the object to the air. He is seventy-seven and starting a second science. Aeroplanes have been flying for five years and nobody yet knows, in numbers, what a wing does.
suggested_refs: Eiffel's drop-test apparatus on the second platform and the first Champ de Mars wind tunnel of 1909

stops.name: Auteuil, the tunnel on the rue Boileau
stops.date_confidence: relocation year attested (fr.wikipedia); month unknown, defaulted. The 1997 classification as a historic monument rests on fr.wikipedia alone and was not independently verifiable
stops.campa: The neighbours of the Champ de Mars complain of the noise, and he moves the laboratory to the rue Boileau in Auteuil and builds a larger tunnel there. French aircraft designers test in it for a generation. He works out the distribution of pressure over wings, publishes the numbers, pays for all of it out of his own pocket and gives the results away. The laboratory is classified a historic monument in 1997 and its tunnel is still turning in the twenty-first century, which no other thing he built can be said to be doing.
suggested_refs: The Laboratoire Aerodynamique Eiffel, 67 rue Boileau, Auteuil, in operation since 1912

stops.name: Paris, the Langley Medal
stops.date_confidence: year attested (en.wikipedia); the precise Paris venue of the ceremony is not confirmed in the sources reached, and the Institut de France pin is a placeholder for an unlocated address. Month unknown, defaulted
stops.campa: The Smithsonian Institution awards him the Samuel P. Langley Medal for aerodromics, and Alexander Graham Bell presents it, saying that Eiffel's writings on the resistance of the air have already become classical. He is eighty-one. The man convicted in 1893 is decorated by the country whose harbour holds his iron pylon under Bartholdi's copper. He goes on publishing tables of resistance for another decade. The exact room in Paris where the medal changes hands is a gap in the record.
suggested_refs: The Samuel P. Langley Medal for Aerodromics, awarded 1913, presented by Alexander Graham Bell

stops.name: Rue Rabelais, the andante
stops.date_confidence: date and street attested (fr.wikipedia, en.wikipedia). Coordinates: the research pool's three lenses give 48.8566/2.3522 (the Paris centroid, about 3 km off), 48.8721/2.3121 and 48.8698/2.3092; the last is used here and the spread is flagged rather than resolved. The Beethoven detail is tradition, given as fact by some sources and as anecdote by others
stops.campa: Gustave Eiffel dies in his house on the rue Rabelais in the eighth arrondissement, ninety-one years old, with Claire keeping the household as she has since she was fourteen. The tradition, printed as fact by some sources and flagged as anecdote by others, is that the andante of Beethoven's Fifth is playing. He has outlived Marguerite by forty-six years, the Panama verdict by thirty, and the demolition date written into his own concession by fourteen. The tower is by then sending the time signal to ships at sea.
suggested_refs: Eiffel's last residence on the rue Rabelais, Paris 8e

stops.name: Saint-Philippe-du-Roule, the funeral
stops.date_confidence: attested (fr.wikipedia)
stops.campa: The funeral is held at Saint-Philippe-du-Roule on the last day of the year, with the government, the engineering schools and the aviators in the pews. During the Panama years several French towns took his name off their streets; the streets have his name back. Twenty-six years from now Claude Levi-Strauss will take up his post at the Musee de l'Homme in the Palais de Chaillot and look at the tower across the river, and Jules Barbier already lies on the hill above it in the cemetery of Passy.
suggested_refs: The Eglise Saint-Philippe-du-Roule, Paris 8e, funeral of 31 December 1923

stops.name: Levallois-Perret, the family vault
stops.date_confidence: same-day burial attested (fr.wikipedia). Coordinates corrected: the cemetery is at about 48.9000/2.2889, and the research pool's three figures (48.8935/2.2833, 48.8935/2.2868, 48.8935/2.288) are all roughly 0.8 km off
stops.campa: He is buried the same day in the family vault in the cemetery of Levallois-Perret, beside Marguerite, a few streets from the workshops where the iron was cut and numbered for four continents. The commune is a factory suburb. The bridges of Porto and Budapest were made here, and the statue in New York harbour, and the tower on the Champ de Mars. The man goes into the ground in the industrial quarter; the monument keeps the address in the centre of the city, which is the arrangement he spent his life building.
suggested_refs: The Eiffel family vault, Cimetiere de Levallois-Perret

stops.name: Champ de Mars, the bust at the north leg
stops.date_confidence: attested (en.wikipedia)
stops.campa: Antoine Bourdelle's bust of Eiffel is unveiled at the foot of the north leg, six years after his death and forty years after the tower opened. Under the concession he signed, the iron above the bust should have been scrap for twenty years by now. The wind tunnel at Auteuil is still running and the Garabit arch is still carrying trains. The name a court allowed him to shorten in 1880 belongs to the tower, and the tower belongs to the city that petitioned against it.
suggested_refs: Antoine Bourdelle's bust of Gustave Eiffel, north leg of the Eiffel Tower, unveiled 2 May 1929
